newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says no agreement before U.S. summit.
newsitem.headline: Israel says no agreement before U.S. summit.

text.p: Israel said no agreements had been reached with the Palestinians ahead of U.S. President Bill Clinton's call on Sunday for an Arab-Israeli summit in Washington this week to salvage peace moves.

"There are none...There is only one understanding, that we're going to Washington," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh told Israel's Channel One when asked if there were any understandings reached.
"From there the call will go out for an end to the violence and acceleration of the negotiations and the return of the sides to intensive negotiations," Naveh said.
In an announcement on the White House lawn on Sunday, Clinton said he hoped to convene a summit following violence that has claimed 69 lives.

PLO officials said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had not officially replied to the U.S. invitation. He wanted Egypt's Hosni Mubarak to attend the summit but the Egyptian leader has not said whether he will attend.
"We have not accepted yet because we do not know whether Mubarak is going," a PLO official said.
"There is an invitation by Mr Clinton. It has not arrived officially and we will make a decision once we receive it," Palestinian cabinet minister Nabil Shaath told reporters.
"I think that we are closer to an agreement more than we were before," Shaath said, adding preparations had to be completed such as the number of invitees and the agenda.
Asked if Palestinians had received assurances, Shaath said: "That is part of what is being discussed now."

Netanyahu's office said the prime minister would leave for Washington on Monday for meetings on Tuesday and Wednesday with Clinton, Jordan's King Hussein, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak should he attend.

"The prime minister welcomes the American initiative on the summit in Washington. The prime minister's position was that this meeting had to be organised with American participation in order to bring concrete results, to end the violence in the area and to accelerate the peace negotiations," the statement said.

"Israel welcomes the acceptance of this position. The prime minister will leave tomorrow...in the afternoon for Washington and on Tuesday and Wednesday will hold meetings with President Clinton, the king of Jordan, Chairman Arafat and President Mubarak if he comes.
"The prime minister hopes that this meeting will indeed bring concrete results: an end to the violence in the area and the renewal of the peace negotiations," the statement said.

Asked Washington's view of the fate of the Jerusalem tunnel which sparked the violence, U.S. Ambassador to Israel, Martin Indyk told Israel Radio: "We are not going before this meeting to get into particular issues."

Asked whether he expected the summit to end with a detailed timetable for Israel's long-delayed redeployment from Hebron, Indyk said: "It's very difficult now to speculate about what the outcome will be and I am not going to do that and I hope you'll understand that.
"I think that what's important is that we now have a way for the two sides to re-engage at the highest levels with the direct involvement of the president of the United States."
